questions.question: Compare the free market, planned and mixed economies through the three questions, justify South Africa's dualistic label, and match each factor of production to its reward.
questions.expected_answer: Every economy answers what, how and for whom; systems differ by who answers. Free market: prices and profit answer — efficient, innovative, wide choice, but unequal, undersupplying public goods and ignoring externalities. Planned: the state answers — equitable on paper but without price signals, producing shortages beside surpluses, weak incentives and slow innovation. Mixed: markets allocate most goods with the state taxing, regulating and providing — every real economy. South Africa is also dualistic: a first-world financial and industrial economy beside a large informal and subsistence economy. Factors and rewards: natural resources earn rent; labour earns wages, its quality raised by education and health; capital — man-made means of production, not money itself — earns interest; entrepreneurship, which combines the others and carries the risk, earns profit — the residual left after the other rewards, which can be negative.

questions.question: Explain price elasticity of demand — calculation, categories and determinants — and show how it decides the effect of a price change on total revenue, then state the profit-maximising rule for a price-taking firm.
questions.expected_answer: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price: above one elastic, below one inelastic, one unitary, plus the perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic endpoints. Determinants: availability of substitutes above all, necessity versus luxury, share of income, and time. Revenue payoff: with inelastic demand a price rise raises total revenue because little quantity is lost — bread, petrol, electricity; with elastic demand a price rise bleeds revenue and a price cut can raise it — products with many substitutes. For costs: fixed costs are unchanged by output, variable costs rise with it, and marginal cost is the cost of the next unit. A price taker's marginal revenue equals the market price, so profit is maximised at the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost — each earlier unit adds profit, each later unit subtracts — verified in a table by comparing the MR and MC columns.

questions.question: Compare monetary and fiscal policy — drivers, instruments, transmission, speed and targets — and explain how the two policies reach the same economy.
questions.expected_answer: Monetary policy: the independent South African Reserve Bank, primary mandate price stability with inflation targeted between three and six percent, instrument the repo rate. Raising it transmits through prime to costlier loans, less borrowing and spending, cooling demand and easing inflation at the cost of slower growth; cutting it reverses the chain, and it can move in an afternoon. Fiscal policy: the elected government through the annual budget, instruments government spending and taxation. Spending injects demand directly; taxation withdraws and redistributes; a deficit is financed by borrowing that accumulates as public debt whose interest bill crowds future budgets; budgets move yearly. Targets differ — inflation for the SARB; growth, jobs and redistribution for the fiscus. Both hands steer one economy, and a full answer names the policy mix, ideally pulling the same way.
